1bit serve: the engine behind one OpenAI-compatible API#

The engine runs inside Lemonade (Lemonade) as a backend, the way Lemonade runs llama-server. Lemonade runs 1bit serve, and for a GGUF it starts the llama-server that serve names, one HTTP hop (below). On HRX the whole graph runs on the GPU or the model does not load: 43 of 43 configurations in the 2026-10-20 census had 0 nodes off HRX. 1bit serve exposes nothing but an OpenAI-compatible API, so it also works on its own with any OpenAI client.

1bit serve -m <model> [--port 8000] [--host 127.0.0.1]
           [--device auto|npu|hrx|hybrid|cpu|ds4] [--ctx-size N] [--alias NAME]
           [--llama-server PATH] [--ds4 PATH] [--ssd-streaming] [--hrx-libhsa PATH]
           [--prefill-provider PATH]      --device hybrid: NPU prefill, HRX decode (docs/hybrid.md)
           [--hrx-cwsr-placement=auto|on|off]
           [--mtp HEAD.gguf | --dflash DRAFT.gguf | --no-mtp] [--mtp-max N] [--mtp-p-min P] [--mmproj MMPROJ.gguf]
           [--laya | --laya-model DIR] [--route-policy FILE]
           [--pm [--pm-experts FILE] [--lemonade-url URL]]
           [--moe-slots N|auto] [--moe-subst R] [--moe-prefetch N] [--moe-predict off|router|block]
                                                              # refused in this build, below
           [--parallel N]
           [--embed MODEL.gguf] [--rerank MODEL.gguf]
           [--npu-opt KEY=VALUE ...]
           [--no-mem-check | --mem-check]
           [--watchdog SECS] [--watchdog-prompt-tps N]
           [--strict-device | --no-strict-device] [--placement-report]
           [--print-backend | --print-backend-env]

One model per process:

Endpoint
GET /health, GET /v1/health 503 while the model loads, then 200 while every backend is up and answers its own health route; 503 again if one has exited, does not answer within 1.5 s, or the watchdog found it hung (below)
GET /v1/models the one model (--alias, else the file or directory name)
POST /v1/chat/completions streamed (SSE) or not; a thinking model's <think> block comes back as reasoning_content ("reasoning_format": "none" keeps it in content)
POST /v1/completions
POST /v1/embeddings with --embed (RAG)
POST /v1/rerank with --rerank (RAG)
POST /v1/embeddings or /v1/rerank with --embedding or --reranking: the model itself is an embedding or reranking model
POST /v1/responses OpenAI Responses API, streamed or not (llama-server devices)
POST /tokenize, /detokenize, /apply-template llama-server devices
GET /slots, POST /slots/<id>?action=…, GET /props llama-server devices; slot save and restore answer 501 (llama-server runs without --slot-save-path)
GET /metrics Prometheus text: the engine's own series (GTT, Tctl, CPU fallbacks, program-cache flushes, starts, watchdog kills) on every child-process device, then the backend's own (below)

"llama-server devices" means hrx and cpu. These routes go to the llama-server behind the model, which is how Lemonade's llamacpp backend reaches them (the onebit recipe inherits it). On npu and ds4 they answer 501.

1bit serve has no authentication (SECURITY.md), so it refuses two kinds of request a web page could make with 403: on a loopback --host, any whose Host header is not a loopback name (localhost, 127.x.x.x, [::1]), and on any host, a POST whose Origin is neither a loopback origin nor the server's own. API clients send no Origin. A reverse proxy in front of a loopback serve must pass the upstream host (nginx's default proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host), not the public one.

Will it fit?#

Before any llama-server starts (hrx, cpu, and the --embed / --rerank servers), serve estimates what the model will hold and refuses a load the box has no room for, in one line and in milliseconds, so Lemonade shows the reason instead of an allocation failure or an OOM minutes into the load. ggml-hrx reports free memory equal to total, so llama.cpp's own --fit cannot do this on HRX0.

$ 1bit serve -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --device hrx --mem-check     # strixhalo, 2026-10-12
Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL: fits: need 33.00 GiB (Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf: weights 16.35 + KV/state 16.15 + compute 0.50) at the model's own ctx 262144 (no --ctx-size), free 57.71 GiB (GTT 73.3 of 120.0 GiB free, MemAvailable 57.7 GiB)

A load that does not fit prints the same line as 1bit serve: <model> does not fit: need …; free memory, lower --ctx-size, or pass --no-mem-check and exits 3 before any backend starts. Lemonade's loader logs that line with the exit code and fails the load ("1bit serve failed to start").

The estimate (app/mem_admit.h) reads only the GGUF header, the way tools/mem-budget's mem_budget.py model does:

  • weights: the GGUF's size, every shard;
  • KV: per attention layer, KV heads x (key + value length) x context x the cache type's bytes (-ctk / -ctv, f16 by default). MLA models (kv_lora_rank) cache the latent and the rope dimensions once. Qwen3.5 / 3.8 / Next attend in one layer of full_attention_interval. Per-layer head_count_kv arrays count only the layers with heads. Sliding-window layers count the window per sequence plus a ubatch, with llama.cpp's per-architecture pattern for which layers are windowed (gpt-oss and Gemma 2: every other layer; Gemma 3: 5 of 6).
  • state: the gated delta-net recurrent state, per sequence;
  • compute: 512 MiB (HRX measured 20-505 MiB);
  • extras: a draft or MTP head (-md, with its KV), --mmproj.

The context is --ctx-size (or a recipe's -c). Without one, llama-server takes the model's own on HRX0 (HRX reports its whole pool free, so --fit shrinks nothing), and serve judges that. On the CPU --fit shrinks an unset context, so serve judges llama.cpp's 4096 floor.

Free is min(GTT total - GTT used, MemAvailable) when a backend runs on HRX0, since the GTT pool is the same DRAM, and MemAvailable on the CPU. A load is refused only when the need plus 1 GiB is more than that. Two things grow after load, so they only warn: - the HRX graph-program cache (2-9 GiB as prompt shapes vary); - landing at or above 95 GiB of GTT, where engine #315's faults were seen.

  • --no-mem-check (or ONEBIT_MEM_CHECK=0) skips the check.
  • --mem-check prints the estimate and exits: 0 when it fits, 3 when it does not.
  • A refused load exits with status 3 too.

ctest mem_admit checks the KV and state sizes against HRX0 server logs:

model ctx KV/state
Qwen3-0.6B 4096 448 MiB
GLM-4.7-Flash (MLA) 2048 105.75 MiB
ZAYA1-8B 2048 80 MiB
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 2048 40 + 62.8 MiB

ctest mem_admit_route checks that a sparse 4 TiB GGUF is refused in milliseconds, before any backend starts. On strixhalo (2026-10-12), estimates for 15 model and context pairs agree with mem_budget.py model (KV from llama-fit-params) within 1.1%. The pairs cover Qwen3 0.6B/8B, GLM-4.7-Flash, ZAYA1-8B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, gpt-oss-20b and MiniCPM4-8B, at 2K-262K context.

When a backend hangs#

A hung GPU dispatch (a wedged HRX queue, a #315 fault) stops llama-server's main loop, while its HTTP thread keeps answering /health with 200. So 1bit serve checks two things itself, for the backends it runs as child processes (hrx, cpu, ds4; the in-process NPU route is not covered):

  • /health follows the backend. Once the model is loaded, serve asks each backend's own health route (/health, or /v1/models for DwarfStar) and answers 503 with the reason when one has exited, does not answer within 1.5 s (Lemonade's probe gives up at 2 s), or the watchdog below has fired. Lemonade's BackendWatchdog probes this route.
  • A progress watchdog. Every chat, completion and Responses request serve forwards is tracked. Progress is a byte from the backend on that request, or the backend's main loop answering GET /slots, which serve asks every few seconds while requests are in flight (llama-server answers it only between decode steps). A request with no progress for --watchdog seconds (default 120; $ONEBIT_WATCHDOG_SECS sets the default; 0 turns it off) means the backend is hung. Before a request's first byte it gets prompt tokens / --watchdog-prompt-tps seconds more (default 50 tok/s; tokens are estimated as request bytes / 4), so a long prompt is not taken for a hang.

When the watchdog fires, serve logs the request, how long it waited, the CPU's Tctl and the backend's last stderr lines (serve passes the backend's stderr through and keeps its tail, which is where an HSA status shows up), SIGKILLs the backend and exits with status 1. Lemonade then sees the backend process gone and loads the model again. A process that does not die after SIGKILL (stuck in the kernel) is reported as such; serve exits anyway.

A lost GPU. After a GPU reset (an MES hang, a MODE2 reset), a backend keeps running but cannot use the device again: ggml-hrx logs AMDGPU hardware exception and llama-server answers every request with HTTP 500 "Compute error". Serve watches the backend's stderr for that line (and Vulkan's device-lost error) and treats it like the watchdog firing, whatever --watchdog is set to: it logs the line, kills the backend and exits with status 1, so systemd (Restart=always) or Lemonade starts it again on the reset device.

1bit serve: watchdog: POST /v1/chat/completions (streamed) on the hrx backend (port 34901, pid 3672241) made no progress for 121 s (limit 120 s; 211 bytes received in 125 s); killing it and exiting so Lemonade reloads it
1bit serve: watchdog: Tctl 71.5 C
1bit serve: watchdog: the backend's last lines:
1bit serve: watchdog: | ...

How this meets Lemonade's BackendWatchdog (wrapped_server.cpp in our Lemonade fork, which owns the restart policy; serve builds none): - Every 5 s Lemonade checks that the backend process is running. Exiting is serve's signal: Lemonade marks the backend reset and reloads the model on the next request. That request is answered with backend_watchdog_reset ("reloaded automatically on retry"). - During an active request, after 90 s with no activity, Lemonade also probes /health (2 s, status 200 required). After 3 failed probes it stops the backend itself. A wedged llama-server still answers its own /health, so this probe alone does not catch a hung GPU. serve's watchdog exit is what does, within --watchdog seconds plus Lemonade's 5 s poll. - LEMONADE_BACKEND_WATCHDOG_* tune Lemonade's side. onebit_args in a recipe passes --watchdog to serve.

A backend with no /slots (DwarfStar, or a llama-server started with --no-slots) shows progress only by sending bytes, so on those only streamed requests are judged: a long non-streamed answer and a hang look the same from outside. tests/watchdog_serve.sh (ctest watchdog_serve, CI included) checks all of this against tests/fake_backend.py, whose "fake_hang" request stops its stream and its /slots while /health stays 200.

Metrics#

Lemonade's own /metrics already reports, per model: - requests, tokens, time to first token and tok/s (lemonade_model_*); - CPU and memory use; - GTT plus VRAM, as lemonade_vram_used_gb.

So GET /metrics on serve adds only what the engine sees and Lemonade cannot, in Prometheus text (format 0.0.4), on every device serve runs as a child process (hrx, cpu, ds4). The in-process NPU route has none yet. serve's own series come first. The backend's own /metrics follows when it answers one: llama-server is started with --metrics, so its llamacpp:* series follow.

Series What
onebit_up{device} 1; device names the route
onebit_serve_starts_total loads of this model by serve, kept across restarts
onebit_watchdog_kills_total backends the progress watchdog killed, kept across restarts
onebit_backend_exits_total backends that exited on their own, kept across restarts
onebit_program_cache_flushes_total ggml-hrx's "HRX graph program cache over its limit" WARN lines
onebit_cpu_fallback_ops{op} engine #390's load report of ops placed off HRX, per op and op="all"
onebit_gtt_bytes{kind="total"\|"used"} the amdgpu GTT pool HRX allocates from (mem_info_gtt_*)
onebit_gtt_fault_zone 1 when GTT use is at or above 95 GiB, where engine #315's faults were seen
onebit_tctl_celsius CPU Tctl (k10temp)

The log-derived series come from the backend's stderr, which serve passes through unchanged and reads line by line (Linux). A series whose line never came is left out, not reported as 0. The #390 report is read from a line that names "CPU fallback" (or "off HRX"), followed by OP=count, OP xcount or OP: count pairs, or by a total alone. llama-server drops the library's INFO lines at its default verbosity, because they map to its trace level. So the report reaches serve only when it is logged as a WARN or above, as the program-cache flush line is.

Starts, watchdog kills and exits outlive one serve process, because Lemonade restarts a backend by starting 1bit serve again. They are kept per model id in ~/.local/state/1bit/serve/<hash of the id>.json (the file names the model inside; the home directory comes from the user database, not $HOME).

How Lemonade picks them up. Lemonade appends a backend's /metrics to its own when the backend's recipe descriptor sets exposes_prometheus_metrics. Each line is renamed lemonade_llamacpp_<name> and labelled with the model. Our fork's onebit descriptor has it false today, so turning it on is a one-line change in the fork, and it is Lemonade's call. Until then, scrape serve's port directly.

tests/metrics_serve.sh (ctest metrics_serve, CI included) checks every series against tests/fake_backend.py.

One hop from Lemonade (--print-backend)#

For a .gguf on HRX, Lemonade does not need serve in the request path. Lemonade's onebit recipe (our fork, branch 1bit/one-hop) runs serve's command with --print-backend added:

$ 1bit serve -m Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf --port 8001 --device hrx --alias Qwen3-4B-1bit --print-backend
{"argv":[".../llama-server","-m","Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf","--host","127.0.0.1","--port","8001","--metrics","--device","HRX0","-ngl","99","--jinja","--alias","Qwen3-4B-1bit","--cache-reuse","256"],"device":"hrx","env":{"GGML_HRX_REPORT":"1","GGML_HRX_STRICT":"1",...},"port":8001}

serve makes every check it makes before a load (the architecture, memory, the placement flags, recipes) and prints the llama-server it would start, on the port Lemonade chose, as one JSON line on stdout, then exits. Lemonade starts that llama-server itself and forwards to it as it does for its own llamacpp recipe: one HTTP hop and two processes (lemond, llama-server) instead of two hops and three.

Exit Meaning Lemonade
0 the plan is on stdout starts it
3 the model does not fit (above) fails the load with serve's line in its log
5 the route needs serve in the request path: an NPU model directory, --device npu, hybrid or ds4, --pm, --laya, --embed or --rerank runs 1bit serve as before

Any other exit (an older engine without the flag) also falls back to 1bit serve, and LEMONADE_ONEBIT_ONE_HOP=0 in lemond's environment turns one hop off. env lists only variables the caller's environment does not set already, so a value the user set still wins, as under serve.

--print-backend-env prints only env, one NAME=VALUE line each, for a caller that builds the argv itself: lemonade-hrx, the stock Lemonade PPA's HRX recipe on Ubuntu 26.04 (lemonade.md, "Ubuntu 26.04: the PPA's lemond").

What serve did on the request path is the backend's own on this route:

  • Health. llama-server's /health answers 503 while its main loop has work queued and has made no progress for LLAMA_SERVER_HEALTH_STALL_SECS (30 s; llama.cpp fork #111), so Lemonade's BackendWatchdog probe (above, When a backend hangs) now catches a hung GPU: three failed probes, and Lemonade stops the backend and reloads the model on the next request.
  • A lost GPU. llama-server exits with status 1 when ggml-hrx logs AMDGPU hardware exception (llama.cpp fork, tools/server/server-device-lost.cpp; LLAMA_SERVER_EXIT_ON_DEVICE_LOST=0 keeps it up), the same signal serve's #466 exit gave Lemonade.
  • Placement. Strict placement, the default on hrx (below), is GGML_HRX_STRICT=1 in the plan's env, so the llama-server Lemonade starts aborts on the first node off HRX, naming it, and Lemonade fails the load with that line in its log. --no-strict-device (or ONEBIT_STRICT_DEVICE=0, or GGML_HRX_STRICT=0 in lemond's environment) leaves it out. serve's own summary line and onebit_* metrics are not printed on this route; llama-server's --metrics still are.
  • Names. --alias gives replies Lemonade's model name; reasoning_content is llama-server's own (--jinja).
  • Prefix reuse. --cache-reuse 256 lets llama-server shift a cached prefix into place when the middle of a conversation changes. A recipe's own --cache-reuse wins.
  • Warm-up. serve sends a backend two synthetic requests once it is ready (HRX only): a chat request (a 360-token prompt, 8 tokens, temperature 0, cache_prompt off), so the first client request does not pay HRX's one-time per-shape program build (#492), and a 16-token /completion prompt (" a" x 16, n_predict 0), below. On this route the plan carries them as "warmups": [{"path", "body"}, ...] (and "warmup", the first one, for an older lemond), on hrx chat plans only; Lemonade's onebit recipe sends them in order after /health answers and before it marks the model loaded. ONEBIT_NO_WARMUP=1 in lemond's environment leaves them out of the plan, as it turns serve's own warm-up off.

Why the 16-token request. The first batch of 13 to 20 tokens after a load takes ggml-hrx's small-batch matmul kernels, which read the weights in a layout ggml-hrx builds on the host the first time it is needed: it re-quantizes the affected tensors (Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL: 6.1 s of CPU time, +1.0 GiB of GTT, held for the life of the server). A chat request is split into batches at the last user message and before its last 4 tokens, so short chats land in that range: Lemonade's chat-short prompt (67 tokens) runs as 50 + 13 + 4. First-request prompt time per length on a fresh server (Qwen3.8-27B, JIT cache warm, 4 cores): 1-12 tokens 0.1-0.5 s, 13-20 tokens 2.03-2.07 s, 21-512 tokens 0.45-1.23 s, rising with the length. The extra request moves that build to load time: +2.1 s per load on the 27B, +0.2 s on Qwen3.5-4B. Outputs are unchanged (greedy chats with and without it are identical; it changes when the layout is built, not which kernels run).

Lemonade's standard benchmark (lemonade bench --scenarios chat-short code-short --runs 5 --warmup 1, a reload before every run, one hop, lemond on cores 0-3), 2026-10-21, TTFT ms:

model chat-short before -> after code-short before -> after
Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL (MTP on) 2,643 -> 796 824 -> 818
Qwen3.5-4B UD-Q4_K_XL 263 -> 138 268 -> 142

Decode is unchanged (27B 25.6 / 29.3 -> 26.2 / 29.6 tok/s, 4B 61.3 / 61.0 -> 61.5 / 60.9). The host build runs one thread per hardware thread, limited by the cores the backend may run on; these numbers are with 4 (not measured unpinned). - Residency. Keeping the model loaded, and so its HRX graph-program cache warm, is Lemonade's: lemonade load --pinned (or "pinned": true), max_loaded_models, and the evict_idle_timeout recipe option when auto_evict is on. A reload starts a new llama-server, whose program cache starts cold.

Measured on Strix Halo, 2026-10-20 (performance mode), with tools/onehop_bench.py: Lemonade fork 23972095 (lemond), engine 1e9de48 (1bit), the llama-server of package 1bit-hrx-3092596 (llama.cpp 00f2a68de, sha256 5c3669cdf3c4104e...) for both arms, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 Q4_K_M (unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-GGUF, sha256 3605803b982cb64a...) on hrx, ctx 8192, with HSA_USERPTR_FOR_PAGED_MEM=0 as the services run. Six rounds per arm (three for /tokenize, 200 requests each), alternating arms; each cell is the range of the rounds' medians. Every request opens a new connection, as Lemonade's client does.

tools/onehop_bench.py --arm two --out out --lemond lemond --onebit build/1bit --llama-server <llama-server>
tools/onehop_bench.py --arm one --out out --lemond lemond --onebit build/1bit --llama-server <llama-server>
two hops (LEMONADE_ONEBIT_ONE_HOP=0) one hop llama-server direct
processes for the model 1bit serve + llama-server llama-server
load, /api/v1/load to ready 1.62 s (2.33 s on the first, cold page cache) 1.35-1.56 s
/tokenize (no GPU work: the hops alone) 0.53-0.64 ms 0.36-0.39 ms 0.11-0.15 ms
1-token chat 19.9-21.5 ms 19.3-21.0 ms 17.5-19.4 ms
time to first token, repeated prompt (prompt cache hit) 19.9-21.1 ms 19.3-21.4 ms
time to first token, fresh 333-word prompt, seen length 116.7-125.3 ms 115.1-119.8 ms

The serve hop cost about 0.2 ms a request, under the run-to-run noise of a GPU request: one hop removes a process and a quarter second of load, not latency anyone sees. The time to first token is the GPU's.

Reload, one hop (three rounds): a prompt length the server had seen answered its first token in 105.6-118.5 ms after Lemonade was asked to load the model again (pinned) and loaded a second model (Qwen3-0.6B Q4_0) beside it: the same llama-server, its program cache warm. After an unload and a load, a new llama-server answered the same length in 227.5-235.7 ms, then about 150 ms and 120 ms as its program cache filled.

tests/print_backend.sh (ctest print_backend, CI included) checks the plan and the exit codes without a GPU.

Model --device Runs on
NPU model directory (model.q4nx + npu/, docs/npu.md) auto, npu the NPU engine, in process (in progress)
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4NX directory (model_type qwen3_5_moe) auto, npu a closed NPU add-on route, in process, in builds with -DONEBIT_NPU_PRIVATE (NPU engine)

Off-HRX placement: strict by default#

Engine #390. HRX could leave part of a graph on the CPU - an op its kernels did not serve, a GET_ROWS outside the supported range - and the model still answered, slower, with nothing said so. The HRX census of 2026-10-20 closed with every runnable cell (43 of 43) all on HRX in every graph, so a node off HRX is now a bug to report, not a fallback to take: on hrx serve refuses it.

The default. Every hrx backend serve starts (the model's own, an --embedding or --reranking model, and the --embed / --rerank servers beside it) gets GGML_HRX_STRICT=1. ggml-hrx checks each graph the scheduler places and aborts on the first node off HRX, naming it, and serve exits non-zero with its own line:

.../ggml-hrx.cpp:447: placement_observer: GGML_HRX_STRICT=1: "kq-0" is MUL_MAT f32 ne=[2,2,12,1] and is not placed on HRX; 12 of 152 nodes off HRX (MUL_MAT x 8, SOFT_MAX x 4), 9 splits
1bit serve: HRX strict placement refused the model: "kq-0" is MUL_MAT f32 ne=[2,2,12,1] and is not placed on HRX; 12 of 152 nodes off HRX (MUL_MAT x 8, SOFT_MAX x 4), 9 splits. Pass --no-strict-device (or set ONEBIT_STRICT_DEVICE=0) to run those nodes on the CPU instead

(jina-reranker-v1-tiny-en Q8_0 with --reranking, on a llama-server built before the jina-bert attention kernels, census gap G10; Strix Halo, 2026-10-20. With --no-strict-device the same load serves /v1/rerank.)

The load, the warmup graph and every later graph are checked. A graph that only a request schedules (a --parallel N multi-sequence batch, a long prompt) therefore aborts at that request, and serve exits with the same line, so Lemonade sees the backend go. The same holds on the one-hop route: the plan's env carries GGML_HRX_STRICT=1. The default needs no extra log volume: the abort is an error line, and the backend keeps its default verbosity. --device cpu and the other devices are not affected.

The opt-out. --no-strict-device, or ONEBIT_STRICT_DEVICE=0 in serve's environment, leaves GGML_HRX_STRICT unset, and HRX runs any node it declines on the CPU, as before. A GGML_HRX_STRICT you set yourself wins over either (0 off, 1 on), under serve and in the one-hop plan.

--placement-report passes GGML_HRX_REPORT=2, so the backend reports every graph, and serve prints its own line whenever a graph has more nodes off HRX than every graph before it:

placement_observer: placement: 512 nodes, 34 off HRX (MUL_MAT x 30, GET_ROWS x 4), 7 graph splits
1bit serve: HRX placement: 34 of 512 nodes off HRX (GET_ROWS x 4, MUL_MAT x 30), 7 graph splits

A graph that is all on HRX prints 1bit serve: HRX placement: all 512 nodes on HRX, 1 graph splits; with , worst of N graphs when more than one reported. The same numbers are onebit_cpu_fallback_ops{op} in Metrics (op="all" is the total). The warmup graph alone is not the model: the census found LFM2 --parallel 4 (20 nodes, 5 splits) and ZAYA1-8B (1-3 nodes) clean in the warmup report and split in prompt and multi-sequence graphs. To see the counts for a model that strict mode refuses, pass --no-strict-device --placement-report. Without --placement-report serve keeps GGML_HRX_REPORT=1 (the first graph only), which costs no log volume.

llama-server drops the library's INFO lines below -lv 4 (an INFO line is a trace line there, common/log.cpp), so at its default verbosity the report never reaches serve. --placement-report passes -lv 4 to the backend for that load, which prints the report along with the rest of llama.cpp's INFO lines.

--strict-device is the default plus the report: GGML_HRX_REPORT=2 and -lv 4, and if a report arrives and names off-HRX nodes, serve refuses with the same numbers (a backend that reached ready despite GGML_HRX_STRICT). It needs --device hrx or auto; ONEBIT_STRICT_DEVICE=1 is the same. It and --no-strict-device do not combine.

Every flag only sets what the backend already reads (llama.cpp fork #102), and a GGML_HRX_REPORT or GGML_HRX_STRICT in the environment wins over what serve passes. tests/hrx_placement_test.cpp (ctest hrx_placement, CI included) covers the report line, the summary, the strict abort line and the default and opt-out environments with no GPU, and tests/print_backend.sh (ctest print_backend) the plan's env. The hardware gate fails any gate model with a node off HRX.

Removed devices and flags#

On the GPU the engine is pure HRX with HIP kernels; no Vulkan, ROCm backend, Metal, ZINC or CUDA (RFC #213 stage 3, 2026-10-01: HRX + NPU, zero Vulkan, zero ROCm; the core strip, 2026-10-04: no ZINC, so no CUDA; 2026-10-12: no MLX/Metal route). Lemonade ships its own backends for those (Lemonade). serve exits at once, with the reason, when asked for any of these:

Asked for What it was
--device vulkan upstream llama.cpp's release on Vulkan0
--device rocm the ROCmFPX tree's ROCm build on ROCm0
--lean ROCmFPX's ROCmFP4 / ROCmI4 formats
--prefill-device hrx, --prefill-min-tokens Vulkan decode with the prompt prefilled on HRX0 over one shared KV cache
--adaptive, --adaptive-at Vulkan for the first requests, ROCm batching the overflow
--long-model, --long-from long conversations to a Hadamard-rotated Q4_0 on the ROCm W4A4 route
--device zinc, --zinc PATH ZINC (zolotukhin/zinc), a Zig GGUF engine on Vulkan, ROCm or CUDA
--device mlx, --mlx-server PATH lemon-mlx-engine's server (MLX on Metal, Apple Silicon); Lemonade has its own MLX backend

The DFlash2 one-server route (a Hadamard-rotated file with W4A4 prompts and DFlash2 decode on ROCm) went with them, and so did its recipes (rotated-moe-ub1024, rocm-dflash-p-min-0.4), and so did the H32 format it served (tools/hadamard_q4_0.py is removed; serve refuses those files). --dflash itself stays, on HRX and the CPU.

A build without the add-on answers a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B directory saying that its NPU route is not part of this build. --npu-opt KEY=VALUE passes an option through to an add-on route. On a route that keeps its cache between requests, usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens counts the reused prompt tokens and timings.cache says where they came from. On the NPU a streamed request with stream_options.include_usage gets a last chunk with usage and timings, as OpenAI's API sends it.

chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking: false works on every device. The GPU backends apply the model's own chat template. The NPU route emits what Qwen3's template does: an empty think block after the assistant prefix. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it also opens <think>\n when thinking is on, as that model's template does.

For a .gguf the engine starts that server as a private child on a loopback port and forwards the OpenAI routes to it, streaming included. Replies carry the served model name. auto means HRX for GGUF: it met RFC #213's decode gates (docs/hrx.md), and it is the engine's only GPU route. With --laya (or --laya-model DIR), Laya classifies each conversation and the route policy picks the device: the built-in policy sends every class to HRX, long documents included, since HRX prefills Qwen3.8-27B at 335 tok/s pp512 (docs/laya.md). The first turn of a conversation pays about 0.5 s for the decision.

HRX needs TheRock's HSA runtime: the distro libhsa rejects gfx1151's PM4-emulation probe, and then HRX registers no device. serve sets IREE_HAL_AMDGPU_LIBHSA_PATH itself unless you did. It uses --hrx-libhsa, else the build's copy, else the first one under /opt/rocm-therock.

The child binaries default to this build's (-DONEBIT_HRX, -DONEBIT_DS4), then $ONEBIT_LLAMA_SERVER / $ONEBIT_DS4, then llama-server / ds4-server on PATH.

Stopping serve (SIGTERM, SIGINT) sends each backend SIGTERM and waits ONEBIT_BACKEND_STOP_GRACE_S seconds (default 30) before SIGKILL, with a warning line first; a backend that already exited is reaped where serve noticed, so its stop is free. A backend that exits on its own ends serve with exit code 1 and the way it ended on stderr (a cpu backend exited: signal 6). The grace matters for a backend that holds an NPU hardware context: it must get to close it itself.

The Project Manager (--pm)#

--pm makes the served model the Project Manager (Project Manager): on /v1/chat/completions it runs a tool loop instead of a plain forward. The model answers general conversation itself and delegates a task that fits an expert's domain with delegate(expert, task, context); the engine turns that into one chat request to Lemonade (--lemonade-url; the onebit recipe passes Lemonade's own address, and by hand the default is http://127.0.0.1:8000, not Lemonade's default port 13305, so pass it) for the expert's catalog id, Lemonade loads the expert beside the PM, and the expert's answer comes back as the tool result. The experts are listed in config/pm-experts.json (built in; --pm-experts FILE replaces it). At most pm.max_rounds (4) rounds; a Lemonade that is down becomes a tool result that says so, and the PM answers alone. Every other route forwards unchanged. Lemonade's catalog entry ZAYA1-8B-PM-1bit runs this (recipe option onebit_pm).

Images (--mmproj)#

--mmproj <mmproj.gguf> hands llama-server a vision projector on the llama.cpp routes (hrx, cpu; auto picks the CPU until HRX vision is checked). Chat messages may then carry image_url parts (a data: URL or a file URL), which llama.cpp's mtmd encodes and places in the prompt. The mmproj comes from convert_hf_to_gguf.py --mmproj on the same checkpoint as the model. With it, llama-server runs with -b 4096 -ub 4096: an image is decoded as one ubatch, which models that attend to an image bidirectionally (ZAYA1-VL, Gemma 3) need. Zyphra's Zamba2-VL and ZAYA1-VL-8B were checked on the removed Vulkan build (vulkan.md at 0baf286). The NPU and DwarfStar routes take no --mmproj.

Greedy requests (temperature 0)#

A request with temperature: 0 (or any negative temperature) leaves nothing to sample: serve forwards it with top_k: 1, so llama-server takes the argmax and skips the top-p / min-p passes over the whole vocabulary. On a 262147-entry vocabulary those passes cost about 2.1 ms per token, which is most of the decode step on a small model: ZAYA1-8B Q4_K_M goes from 118 to 153 tok/s at temperature 0, and Qwen3.8-27B gains in proportion to its own vocabulary (248320 entries).

A request that names its own top_k keeps it — only the absent case is filled in — and a request with any other temperature is forwarded untouched, so sampling behaviour is unchanged everywhere it matters. tests/greedy_shortcut.sh (ctest greedy_shortcut) pins all four cases against tests/fake_backend.py without a GPU.

Multi-token prediction (--mtp)#

--mtp <head.gguf> turns on llama-server's draft-mtp speculative decoding: the model's own MTP head (Unsloth ships it as MTP/mtp-<model>-*.gguf) drafts tokens on the same device, and the model checks them in one batch. --mtp-max N caps the draft length; --mtp-p-min P drafts a token only when the head is at least that sure of it. It works on the llama.cpp devices (hrx, cpu), and --device auto keeps it on HRX0. A drafted token is kept only when the model agrees, so the output is the model's own.

A GGUF's own MTP head is on by default on hrx. When the -m file carries its MTP layer (<architecture>.nextn_predict_layers > 0, e.g. Unsloth's Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL, blk.64.nextn.*) and no other drafter is asked for, serve adds --spec-type draft-mtp with no -md: llama-server loads the head from the model file. That is what Lemonade's own llamacpp recipe does for a model with the mtp label, which Lemonade sets from the same key; both 1bit serve and the one-hop plan do it. --mtp-max and --mtp-p-min apply. Not on cpu, not with --parallel > 1, not for --embedding / --reranking, and --no-mtp (or ONEBIT_NO_MTP=1; Lemonade: onebit.args=--no-mtp) turns it off. A file without the key is unchanged.

Lemonade's standard benchmark (lemonade bench --scenarios chat-short code-short --runs 5 --warmup 1, the pinned CI's protocol, a reload before every run), onebit recipe on the one-hop route, Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL, Strix Halo, 2026-10-21 (decode tok/s, chat-short / code-short):

tok/s TTFT ms
no drafter (before) 11.1 / 11.9 2298 / 724
own MTP head (now) 24.9 / 29.1 2424 / 807
own MTP head + one-hop warm-up 26.2 / 29.5 2446 / 824
Lemonade's llamacpp Vulkan, same file, --spec-type draft-mtp (README of the 2026-10-21 run) 24.2 / 28.0 1882 / 1882

Greedy outputs with and without the head (three 128-token chats): two identical, one diverges at a near-tie (" Earth" -0.684 against " the" -0.705 without MTP), where the verify batch's numerics pick the other token; a drafted token is still only kept when the model's verify pass agrees.

On HRX, Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL with its MTP head (default draft length 3, greedy 256-token chats, medians of 3 fresh servers) decodes at 36.0 / 26.8 / 29.9 tok/s on code / prose / short, up from 25.9 / 20.5 / 21.9, since our HIP kernels check 2 to 8 drafted tokens in one pass: the 4-token verify step went from 121.5 to 88.0 ms (#487). Without MTP it decodes at 12.15 tok/s (tg128, HRX).

The sweep below was taken on the removed Vulkan build (2026-09-24) and is kept for the settings it found; it has not been repeated on HRX. The sweep (draft length x --mtp-p-min, code / prose / short; 12.2 / 12.3 / 12.3 without MTP):

Setting tok/s Drafts accepted
--mtp (draft length 3, the default) 35.9 / 28.2 / 28.8 94% / 68% / 75%
--mtp-max 4 --mtp-p-min 0.5 38.1 / 28.0 / 26.9 93% / 71% / 76%
--mtp-max 6 --mtp-p-min 0.5 42.0 / 27.3 / 25.2 84% / 60% / 72%
--mtp-max 8 21-25 / 13-20 / 10-20 76-88% / 39-65% / 33-78%

Use the default for chat and --mtp-max 6 --mtp-p-min 0.5 for code (3.4x): code is predictable enough to keep long drafts, prose is not. Draft length 8 collapses on every prompt. Adding n-gram drafting to MTP gains nothing.

Cap the draft on HRX: config/recipes.json pins --mtp-max 3 for qwen35 on hrx, which is also llama-server's default — 32.6 / 26.9 / 28.0 tok/s on the 27B on 2026-10-24. Do not raise it past 7: from 8 drafts on, acceptance falls to 0.17-0.60 and the longer verify batch costs more than the drafts return (--mtp-max 7 --mtp-p-min 0: 37.9 / 22.4 / 22.4; --mtp-max 15: 33.6 / 14.9 / 13.5, even with 16-token verify kernels). Code is the one case where a longer draft still pays, and only up to 7. Small-active MoE models are the opposite case: on Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (3B active, 88 tok/s then) every draft model tried (Qwen3 0.6B / 1.7B / 4B) was slower than no drafting, even at 82-87% acceptance.

Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B: the Qwen3.8 head, and two drafts by default#

PrismML's Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B is a qwen35 model with ternary weights, and its three published files (PTQ1_0, PQ2_0, the packed Q4_0) hold the same weights: the 4096 blocks we compared decode identically, so picking a file is picking a size, not a model. PQ2_0 is the pick — 9.8 GiB against 17.2 for the packed Q4_0, and the fastest of the three at both ends (pp512 553, tg128 21.4 tok/s, against 237/19.0 and 176/16.1).

Because the geometry is Qwen3.8's, Qwen3.8-27B's own MTP head attaches to it: --mtp MTP/mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf drafts and the ternary model verifies. That head is the recommendation — PQ2_0 with MTP decodes at 43 / 37 / 27 tok/s on code / prose / short (39/40 on GSM8K, against 20-21 tok/s without drafting), and a DFlash2 drafter works on it too since llama.cpp fork #143 but trails the MTP head (0.37 against 0.67 acceptance), so it is not the pick here.

The ternary files accept 0.76 of two-token drafts against 0.67 at three, so the draft length is 2 for prose, short answers and translation and 4 when the traffic is code (40.4 / 38.3 / 30.4 / 34.7 tok/s at two drafts over code / prose / short / translation, 43.7 / 36.0 / 24.6 / 30.1 at four). config/recipes.json pins the 2-draft default for these files only: the recipe matches on the PrismML metadata key the Hadamard-folded files carry (prism.hadamard.version), so it cannot catch a plain Qwen3.8-27B, which has the same architecture. Raising the draft length is --mtp-max 4.

Both the PQ2_0 dense prefill kernels and the ternary verify kernels come with the next private-add-on pin; on the current one, PQ2_0 prefill runs at 188 tok/s instead of 553.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: drafting from part of the vocabulary#

Flash-Next's MTP head computes logits over all 248,320 tokens for every drafted token. That is the model's 644 MiB Q8_0 output matrix, read three times per decode step at draft length 3. A draft only proposes; the model checks every token, so the head can be cut down to the tokens it is likely to propose. tools/mtp_draft_vocab.py writes such a head from Unsloth's shared head file and the model's own output rows. Our llama.cpp fork (qwen4exp, src/models/qwen4exp-draft-vocab.cpp) runs it on HRX since pin e57beb97:

python3 tools/mtp_draft_vocab.py \
  --mtp MTP/mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-shared-Q8_0.gguf --target UD-Q4_K_XL/ \
  --ids config/draft-vocab/qwen38-en-code-65536.txt --out mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-dv65k.gguf

config/draft-vocab/qwen38-en-code-65536.txt is dime-online's 65,536-id list, picked from English prose and source code (qwen3.8-Flash-DGX-UltraFast, Apache-2.0, see NOTICE). It makes the head 170 MiB.

Measured with the fork's Vulkan llama-server on Strix Halo, 2026-10-01. Settings: - UD-Q4_K_XL, greedy, draft length 3, -lm mmap -lzm on - decode tok/s, median of rounds 2-3 of 3

Prompt Full head 65,536-id head
code, 256 tokens 47.8 52.1
prose, 256 tokens 38.6 42.2
code, 768 tokens 45.8 48.3
French, 26 tokens 46.4 39.6
  • English and code: 8-9% faster, the same acceptance, and about 6 ms less per decode step (76 -> 70 ms).
  • Other languages: text outside the list loses, as the French row shows. Use the full head for such text.
  • Output text: decoding with a draft is not token-identical to decoding without one, even with the full head. Batched verification flips near-ties (one flip each in prose and long code here). The cut head gives the full head's text in rounds 2-3, with two other flips in round 1.
  • Q4_K_M: Unsloth's shared Q4_K_M head was no faster and flipped more often.
  • -lm mmap: Flash-Next needs it on this llama.cpp. Without it, the 27.5 GiB per-layer embedding table is copied into RAM next to the ~82 GB the GPU holds, which does not fit in 128 GB.

DFlash draft models (--dflash)#

Not on this pin. On llama.cpp pins before fork e91b608cd (this one, and the release candidate built on it) a DFlash2 drafter fails to load with done_getting_tensors: wrong number of tensors; expected 81, got 58; fixed by fork #139 + #140, lands with the next pin bump.

--dflash <draft.gguf> uses a DFlash block-diffusion draft model instead of the MTP head: the draft emits a whole block of tokens in one pass, reading the model's hidden states, and the model checks the block in one batch. It turns on llama-server's draft-dflash (DFlash2's candidate selector included). A drafter is trained for one target model; z-lab publishes them on Hugging Face (for example z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2, 2B, Apache-2.0). --dflash and --mtp are exclusive. --mtp-max and --mtp-p-min set the draft length and threshold for either; without --mtp-max, --dflash drafts full blocks (llama-server's own default of 3 throws most of the gain away).

Convert the drafter with upstream llama.cpp's converter. It needs only the target's config.json and tokenizer files, not its weights:

hf download Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B --include "*.json" "*.jinja" "merges.txt" "vocab.json" --local-dir Qwen3.8-27B-hf
hf download z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 --local-dir DFlash2
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py DFlash2 --target-model-dir Qwen3.8-27B-hf --outtype bf16 --outfile dflash2-bf16.gguf
llama-quantize dflash2-bf16.gguf dflash2-q8_0.gguf Q8_0
1bit serve -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf --dflash dflash2-q8_0.gguf

Measured through 1bit serve on Strix Halo on 2026-10-24: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL, the same three chat prompts as above (code / prose / short, decode tok/s), greedy 256-token answers, medians of three fresh servers, performance mode, strict placement on — the drafter's candidate selector (its top-k, fill and row-gather nodes) runs on HRX, so the whole drafter graph is on the GPU in one graph split:

Drafter code prose short
none 12.1 12.1 12.5
--mtp (the file's own head, draft length 3) 32.6 26.9 28.0
--dflash (DFlash2 Q8_0, whole blocks) 56.6 30.8 20.6
--dflash (DFlash2 Q4_K, whole blocks) 58.8 — —

DFlash2 is the pick for code (+73% over MTP, 4.7x without drafting) and about level on prose, but a short answer stops before a block is worth filling, so it loses a third there. The default stays MTP for chat; --dflash is for code-heavy serving. Acceptance on the three prompts is 0.88 / 0.42 / 0.23, and a drafted token is kept only when the model's verify pass agrees, so the output is the model's own. The Q8_0 drafter is what the numbers above use; a Q8_0 file is also what the drafter's own README recommends over BF16.

Without --mtp-max, --dflash drafts the drafter's block minus one (its dflash.block_size; 16 when the file does not say). DFlash2's block is 8 tokens, not 16: the seven drafts per verify step are what 1bit serve --dflash asks for, and they fit the 2-8-token verify kernels.

A non-zero draft threshold throws whole blocks away: on the 27B, --spec-draft-p-min 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6 cut prose from 30.8 to 22.5-23.3 tok/s, so config/recipes.json pins --spec-draft-p-min 0 for qwen35 on hrx (docs/recipes.md). --mtp-p-min sets the same threshold. (The DFlash2 one-server route on the lean ROCm build is gone, above.)

Recipes (--recipes, --no-recipes)#

Tuned llama-server settings that depend on the model and route go in config/recipes.json as recipes, each with the measurement behind it. The built-in set has two entries today, both for Qwen3.8-27B on hrx: --spec-draft-p-min 0 with a DFlash2 drafter and --mtp-max 3 with the file's own MTP head (Recipes). Serve prints each recipe it applies. Anything serve sets itself wins over a recipe. --recipes FILE replaces the built-in set and --no-recipes turns recipes off (Recipes). To measure a setting before making it a recipe, use tools/bench.py.

MoE models larger than memory: not in this build#

--moe-slots is kept (the option, --moe-subst, --moe-prefetch and serve's code for them), but the expert streamer lives in the removed Vulkan llama.cpp pin. Until it moves to HRX together with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, serve refuses --moe-slots with "not available in this build". What follows describes it as it ran on Vulkan0 (docs/moe-streaming.md).

--moe-slots N keeps a MoE model's routed experts in the file and holds N of them, across all layers, in GPU memory. Decode reads the missing ones from the drive as the router picks them. The rest of the model loads on the GPU as usual.

1bit serve -m Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf --moe-slots 4608 --ctx-size 8192

Qwen3-Coder-30B has 6,144 experts; at 4,608 slots it decodes 39 tok/s warm, at 1,536 about 6-7 (docs/moe-streaming.md, "Streaming in the inference path"). A model that fits in memory is faster without it (79-91 tok/s resident).

--moe-subst R trades a little accuracy for fewer reads: when the router picks an expert that is not in memory, a resident one among its next choices takes its place if it scores at least R times as high. 0.5 cut Coder-30B's drive reads by 20-27% and sped decode up 10-35% at 1,536 and 3,072 slots, for a KL divergence of 0.008-0.012 against the exact model (docs/moe-streaming.md, "Routing that prefers resident experts"). Without it, routing is exact.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q4_K_XL (111 GB) runs this way from 18-32 GiB of GPU memory: 3.5-6 tok/s exact at 4,608-9,216 slots. On that model use --moe-subst 0.9 or none: 0.5 costs a KL divergence of 0.07 there.

--moe-slots auto sizes the cache from free memory: MemAvailable, less the other tensors the GPU holds and a reserve (8 GiB or 15%), divided by the model's mean expert size. On a box with 40 GiB free it gave Flash-Next 9,331 of 24,576 experts (27.2 GiB) beside 5.1 GiB of other tensors, and serve held 145 MiB of anonymous memory. Other processes can take that memory back later; on a shared box, give a number instead. The gate-ahead prefetch is off unless --moe-prefetch N asks for it (it doubled Flash-Next's decode time).

Prompts are slow when streaming: a batch larger than 8 tokens runs the experts on the CPU from the mapped file (Flash-Next: 0.4-0.8 tok/s of prompt). Keep prompts short, or see docs/moe-streaming.md, Next.

--moe-predict off|router|block (default off; only with --moe-slots, and a prefetch to predict for means --moe-prefetch 1) chooses what the prefetch predicts the next layer's experts with. block runs the next layer's own mixer block on the current residual, which is what makes the prediction fit Flash-Next's hyper-connections; router keeps the cheap residual-only form. The predictor changes only which experts are read early, never the output (docs/moe-streaming.md, "The next layer's own block"). Untested on device: the predictor and its hit-rate table are built and unit-tested host-side, and it needs the HRX streamer to consume it.

Many requests at once (--parallel)#

--parallel N gives llama-server N slots (-np N): requests that arrive together decode together, one read of the weights per step for all of them (continuous batching, what vLLM is built on). --ctx-size is split across the slots, so size it for all of them.

On HRX, --parallel N shares one KV cache across the slots (-kvu) so attention stays on the GPU, and turns off AMD's Qwen attention path, which ignores the other sequences. HRX does not yet run a gated delta-net model (Qwen3.5, Qwen3.8, Qwen3-Next) with more than one sequence: serve refuses --parallel > 1 there, and without --parallel gives those models one slot.

The earlier measurements here (Vulkan and ROCm batching, and --adaptive, which ran both) went with those builds (RFC #213 stage 3); see this page at 0baf286. --adaptive and --long-model are refused now (above).

RAG (--embed, --rerank)#

--embed MODEL.gguf serves /v1/embeddings and --rerank MODEL.gguf serves /v1/rerank, each from its own llama-server beside the chat model (--embedding, --reranking, the whole input in one batch). In a build with HRX that server runs on HRX0 with one slot and inputs of up to 2048 tokens (HRX runs one sequence per batch); a build without HRX runs it on the CPU, 4 slots and 8192 tokens. /v1/models lists them with their role. A RAG client embeds its documents, retrieves by cosine similarity, reranks the best few and asks the chat model with them as context, all against the one server:

--embedding and --reranking serve the model itself in that role, as Lemonade loads embedding and reranking models: 1bit serve -m nomic-embed-text-v2-moe.Q8_0.gguf --embedding. They run on hrx or cpu (auto: HRX where the build has it). On Strix Halo (2026-10-02, two repeats each): Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B Q8_0 embeddings repeat bit for bit on HRX; bge-reranker-v2-m3 Q8_0 scores repeat exactly (8.609 / -6.756 / -0.401 / -11.020). jina-reranker-v1-tiny still fails on HRX: its JIT can't link the fp32 matmul-with-bias kernel it needs.

1bit serve -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --mtp mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf \
  --embed Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-Q8_0.gguf --rerank qwen3-reranker-0.6b-q8_0.gguf

Measured end to end on Strix Halo (2026-09-24): the engine's own docs and README as the corpus (93 passages of about 120 words), four questions with known answers, Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL with --mtp answering, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B Q8_0 embedding (queries prefixed with its Instruct: ... Query: line):

Stage Time
Embed the 93 passages 3.4-5.6 s
Embed a question 17-32 ms
Cosine search 4-11 ms
Rerank 8 passages 0.4-0.6 s
Answer (700-1,560-token prompt) 4-5.6 s at 27-33 tok/s
Retrieval Right
Top 8 by embedding, all 8 as context 3/4 (the fourth answered 11.0 ms/token, the same fact as 91 tok/s)
Top 3 by embedding 1/4
Top 8, reranked to 3 by Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B 1/4: it scores every passage 0.96-1.0 through llama.cpp (two conversions tried)
Top 8, reranked to 3 by bge-reranker-v2-m3 0/4: it discriminates, but keeps the wrong passages

So use embeddings with a wide context and no reranker: retrieval is about 25 ms, and a few thousand extra prompt tokens cost little at 270-320 tok/s prefill. --rerank stays for larger corpora, where cutting 50 candidates to 8 matters more.

Verified (Strix Halo, 2026-09-23)#

tests/serve_e2e.sh with Qwen3-0.6B: the Q4_K_M GGUF for the GPU devices and the Q4NX model directory for the NPU. The test checks /health 200, /v1/models, a chat that answers "Paris." under the served name, and streaming:

Device Result
npu PASS (33 SSE chunks): Qwen3-0.6B NPU model directory
hrx PASS (32 SSE chunks), with no environment set up

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on the NPU is tested by its add-on (NPU engine). Without it, serve on that directory exits with the message above.

(The vulkan row, PASS with 32 SSE chunks, went with the Vulkan build, and the zinc row, PASS with 6, with ZINC.) With -DONEBIT_HRX=ON, ctest runs serve_e2e_hrx and serve_e2e_cpu, and in general serve_e2e_<device>, when configured with -DONEBIT_SERVE_TEST_GGUF=<gguf>. smoke_serve runs everywhere, CI included: tests/fake_backend.py stands in for llama-server. It checks the proxy (/health, /v1/models, the reply rename, SSE relay), that no backend outlives a SIGKILLed serve, and that a backend that exits on its own ends serve at once. watchdog_serve runs everywhere too (see "When a backend hangs").

--precise: a follow-up turn is bitwise identical to a cold run#

A follow-up turn in the same conversation is not bit-identical to a cold run of that conversation. The follow-up continues from the KV cache and prefills only its new user message (28 tokens in the test below), where a cold run prefills the conversation in 512-token ubatches - and HRX serves a different token count with a different plan, so the last bits of the logits differ and a near-tie can flip. Measured on 2026-10-22, 10 greedy two-turn chats per model, follow-up against a cold run of the same conversation.

--precise (or ONEBIT_PRECISE=1) makes every request re-prefill its whole conversation, which is exactly the path a cold run takes: with it, 10/10 chats came out identical on Qwen3.8-27B and 9/10 on Qwen3-4B (the remaining 4B difference is at a 0.0385-nat tie with both arms prefilling the same tokens, i.e. a question about that path's determinism rather than about batch size). The cost is the full time-to-first-token of the conversation on every turn instead of only the new tokens: on the 27B a follow-up goes from 672 ms to 4785 ms after a ~1.6k-token conversation and from 676 ms to 12348 ms after ~5.4k tokens. It is off by default, and the token stream of a single turn is unchanged either way.
